intro: Streaming inference sees chunks rather than the whole sequence. Retain just enough history to match a continuous causal convolution.
task: Compute outputs for the new chunk and return the history needed for the next call.
requirements: chunk and kernel are vectors; kernel length is 2..64. state has length kernel_length-1 and stores previous samples from oldest to newest.

For current sample at time t, output=sum(kernel[j]*sample_at_t_minus_j). Thus kernel[0] multiplies the current sample. Return {"output": vector, "state": the last kernel_length-1 samples of concatenated history and chunk}.

Use finite real numeric values of magnitude at most 1e6, excluding boolean inputs. Each array axis has 1..64 entries and at most 65536 elements total unless a stricter bound is stated. Return NumPy arrays for array outputs, preserve caller inputs, and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: Two tap stream
examples.output:
{'output': [7.0, 10.0], 'state': [4.0]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

examples.name: Short chunk retains history
examples.output:

(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

hints.title: Follow the data
hints.body: Join the stored history to the new chunk before applying backward-looking windows.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: A chunk shorter than the kernel still leaves some old history in the next state.

explanation: A finite causal kernel needs only a fixed-length suffix of past input. Carrying that suffix makes chunk boundaries invisible to the mathematical operation.

Kernel orientation is easy to reverse accidentally: the first coefficient corresponds to the newest sample here. Keeping a clear state order enables independent streaming and full-sequence implementations to agree.
